22.s: La Rocca says New Orleans papers disowned the band, and the reader reads a hostile 1918 editorial condemning jazz.
22.q: Look at me here. In 1918, the New Orleans papers, or the Times-Picayune, disowned us, and say that we were not from New Orleans. I'll ask Mr. Eickward to read this, Jazz and Jazzism, which is an editorial that appeared in the New Orleans Times-Picayune, June of 20, 1918. Mr. Eickward, would you…

22.s: La Rocca introduces and the reader reads a letter to the editor answering the editorial.
22.q: Now you can see from there what the people knew at this time about jazz music. They got a lot of people with lip service willing to talk about it, but they weren't here to defend this music. Only Nicola Rocca was here and know about this music. Here's some answers to that same article. Would you…

22.t: More 1918 Times-Picayune letters on ragtime and jazz
22.s: The reader reads further letters to the editor defending ragtime and jazz.
22.q: this is another one here let's take your turn with it

114.t: Critics and what makes a valid criticism
114.s: Asked about critics, Moody says non-players can still judge but should say why, citing Rush as an example.
114.q: Well, I don't -- first of all, they're critics, but there are critics and then there are critics. Now, just because a person can play an instrument -- that doesn't mean that they can say what's good and what isn't because I don't care who it is. All I can do is give you an opinion as to what I…

114.t: Kenny G, critics and musicians as singers
114.s: He says critics must remember musicians have the ears, and jokes about singers pointing to the sax player to scat.
114.q: and they make thousands and thousands upon dollars because other people think it's the goodest thing that there is. You know what I mean? So, could it -- I would look at it this way. If I were going to criticize something, I'd say well, that's not my cup of tea, I don't like it and here's the…

114.t: Critics do environmental listening; no one can tell him how to play
114.s: Most critics only follow reputation, and only another musician can help you play better.
114.q: But the musicians, like, you know, [Scats] I thought I heard something there, you know. But anyway, you know what I mean.

545.t: The critic as consumer guide and mediator; JJA clinics
545.s: He wants to be slightly ahead of readers and mediate between musician and reader, and describes JJA clinics for young journalists.
545.q: I think the consumer guide aspect of jazz journalism is valuable if it functions in that way. I like to be a little bit ahead of my readers. I hope I can suggest things to them that they haven’t though of before. I mean I want to be — not always provocative or inspiring but I want to be more…

512.s: Critics said he was banging or putting people to sleep; he says it was pure sound modeled on nature.
512.q: Oh yeah that’ might happen. Because I remember back then I would play “A Garden of Peace” and some people would say you’re putting me to sleep. Years later. Yeah, okay. But you know oh, a lot of times they said, when we were stretching out and I was using my fingers and my things to get more sound

613.t: Should critics be musicians; writing in plain language
613.s: Playing is not necessary for a critic, with Whitney Balliett as example, and he favors simple words over insider jargon.
613.q: Yeah it’s important for a jazz critic to have as much knowledge as possible, and if you play a little bit of music that’s good. But it’s not necessary. I mean Whitney Balliet, the best of all writers on jazz, he was always my favorite. You could read his reviews and you could almost hear the music…

372.t: Whether the Tristano music was ever a working band
372.s: They return to Gioia and Tristano's influence on musicians rather than public, and whether Lennie wanted a band.
372.q: At some point, I think when we had the professional picture made in uniforms, there was a thought that this might be a working band. So that’s obviously a truth. It wasn’t a working band.
